lines.speaker: Nireus
lines.text: All right, here we are. Menippus can judge which of us is better-looking. Tell me, Menippus: don't I seem the prettier one to you?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And who are you, exactly? I feel we should establish that first.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: So which one is Nireus, and which one is Thersites? That part is not yet obvious.

lines.speaker: Thersites
lines.text: Well, I've got that much already: I look like you. And you aren't ahead of me by anything like the margin Homer — that blind fellow — gave you when he called you the most beautiful of them all. Here I am, bandy-legged and bald-patched, and to the judge I turn out no worse. Still, Menippus, have a look and decide which one you think is handsomer.

lines.speaker: Nireus
lines.text: Me, obviously. Son of Aglaia and Charopus. The man who came to Troy the most beautiful of all.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Yes, but not, I think, the most beautiful man to come underground. The bones are the same. The only way your skull differs from Thersites' skull is that yours is more delicate. Thin, brittle-looking. Not very manly.

lines.speaker: Nireus
lines.text: Ask Homer what I was like when I served with the Achaeans.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You're telling me dreams. I look at what you have now. People back then can deal with back then.

lines.speaker: Nireus
lines.text: So I am not better-looking here, Menippus?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You are not. Nobody is. In Hades we have equality: everyone looks the same.

lines.speaker: Thersites
lines.text: That is quite enough for me.
